### The Bench at the End of the Line

On the last night of the Number 6, someone brought a cake. This was against the rules, but Len had been driving the route for twenty-three years and could no longer remember whether the rule was *no food* or *no hot food*. The cake was cold. He let it on.

“Where do you want it?” asked the woman holding it.

“Is it going to pay?”

“I’ve got exact change.”

She put two coins in the slot. Len printed the cake a ticket, and she carried it to the seat behind him, where it rode all the way downtown with LAST STOP written in blue icing.

At eleven fifteen, the bus was ordinarily empty except for a dishwasher named Ivo, who took his shoes off as soon as he sat down. Tonight, people kept getting on. There was a man Len recognized only when he folded his newspaper into quarters. There were twins who had once been small enough to turn around under the seat without bumping their heads. They were in their thirties now and seemed surprised to see each other.

“Did Mum tell you?” one asked.

“No,” said the other. “Did she tell you?”

They spent three stops trying to establish how they had both found out.

The city had not, strictly speaking, canceled the bus. It had made improvements. Starting Monday, riders could take the 14 to the hospital, cross six lanes of traffic, and catch the 22, which would deliver them almost anywhere the 6 had gone. There was a diagram. Len had studied it long enough to discover that a person could get from his first stop to his last in forty-seven minutes, provided they could walk briskly and the second bus waited while they crossed.

The second bus would not wait. Len knew the driver.

Near the old swimming pool, a girl pulled the cord. Len opened the doors. Nobody moved.

“Sorry,” she said. “I’ve always wanted to do that.”

“You’ve never pulled the cord?”

“My grandmother always did it.”

He shut the doors. In the mirror he watched her wind the sleeve of her sweater around her fingers. He thought he knew which grandmother she meant. For years there had been a woman who pulled the cord immediately after boarding, then looked straight ahead while the bus stopped at every corner between the pool and her house. Eventually she and Len had reached an understanding. She could pull it whenever she liked, and he would let her out at Maple.

At Maple, the girl stayed on.

The last stop was a triangle of cracked pavement between a shuttered florist and the river. The city had bolted a bench there in 1987 and painted it green. In summer, the slats gave off a hot, piney smell. In winter, the bench was a way to get colder than you would have thought possible while wearing pants.

Len pulled in at eleven fifty-eight. Nobody stood.

“What happens to the bench?” the woman with the cake asked.

Len turned off the engine. In the sudden quiet he could hear the river pushing something hollow against the bank.

“I don’t know,” he said.

It was the first question anyone had asked him about the changes that he couldn’t answer. He knew which fares would be honored, where to get a new schedule, and what wording to use if you wanted a real person to read your complaint. He had a card in his pocket with twenty copies of a telephone number, cut into strips because the depot wouldn’t pay to print leaflets. He had not thought to ask about the bench.

The woman peeled the lid off the cake. The icing had stuck to the plastic, leaving only STOP. She passed it around on brown napkins. Someone had brought a knife, but nobody had brought forks.

While they ate, Ivo stepped outside and crouched beside the bench. He came back to ask whether anybody had a socket wrench. The man with the newspaper did, though it took him a while to get it out of the packaging. He had bought it that afternoon to fix a loose toilet seat.

Len watched the two men through the windshield. One held up a phone for light; the other leaned so hard on the wrench that his heels came off the pavement. The first bolt gave with a noise loud enough for everyone on the bus to hear.

“Where are you taking it?” Len asked when they had finished.

This hadn’t occurred to them. They looked down at the bench, which was longer from underneath than it had been from above.

“My grandmother’s building has a laundromat,” the girl said. “People sit on the dryers.”

“That’s back up the route,” said Len.

Nobody pointed out that he knew the way.

The bench wouldn’t fit through the front doors. They got it through the back by turning it on its end, knocking one of the overhead lights loose. Len tucked the light cover into the pocket beside his seat. The twins stood in the aisle and held the bench steady, each bracing a foot against the same iron leg.

On the way back, they passed a man walking a little white dog. He saw the bus and began to run, waving his free hand. Len pulled over.

“Does this go downtown?” the man asked.

“Not anymore,” Len said. “Where are you going?”

The man named a street two blocks from Maple. He started to explain about his car, then about the person who had promised him a ride. Len lowered the bus so the dog could get on.

At the laundromat, there was just enough space for the bench under the window if they moved the trash can. The girl called her grandmother, who came down in slippers and a good wool coat. She put one hand on a slat and rubbed at a pale mark someone had left there long ago with a cigarette.

“You’ll want to put something under that leg,” she said.

The man with the newspaper folded a section into a thick square. Len held the bench up while he pushed it underneath. Then the grandmother sat down, bounced once to see if it would hold, and moved over to make room.
